questions.text: A plane mirror always forms an image that is ____.

options.text: real, inverted, and the same size as the object
virtual, erect, and the same size as the object
real, erect, and diminished in comparison
virtual, inverted, and magnified beyond the object

questions.explanation: Images in plane mirrors are: virtual (cannot be projected on a screen), erect (upright, not flipped top-to-bottom), the same size as the object, and laterally inverted (left-right flip). The image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

questions.text: The bending of a light ray when it passes from air into water is called ____.

options.text: reflection at the water surface interface
diffraction around the water-air boundary
refraction due to change in optical density
dispersion into component wavelengths

questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light at the boundary between two media of different optical densities. Light entering water from air slows down and bends toward the normal because water is optically denser (higher refractive index ~1.33) than air (~1.00).

questions.text: A convex lens is held very close (within its focal length) to a printed page. The image seen by the eye is ____.

options.text: real, inverted, and magnified beyond focal length
virtual, erect, and magnified — acts as a magnifying glass
real, erect, and diminished to a smaller print size
virtual, inverted, and the same size as the original

questions.explanation: When an object is placed between the optical centre and the focal point of a convex lens (u < f), the image formed is virtual, erect, and magnified — the basis of a magnifying glass. A real, inverted image requires the object to be beyond the focal point.

options.text: light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium at any angle
light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle
white light splits into its component colours passing through a prism
light reflects off a concave mirror without any accompanying refraction

questions.explanation: TIR requires two conditions: (1) light must travel from a denser to a rarer medium (e.g., glass to air), and (2) the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. Applications include optical fibres (communications), diamonds (brilliance), and mirages. Option A describes normal refraction, not TIR.

questions.text: In the visible spectrum arranged from violet to red (VIBGYOR), which colour has the highest frequency?

options.text: Red — longest wavelength, lowest energy photons
Green — middle of the visible spectrum range
Yellow — highest intensity in sunlight spectrum
Violet — shortest wavelength, highest frequency

questions.explanation: Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength (f = c/λ). Violet has the shortest wavelength (~380–420 nm) and therefore the highest frequency and energy among visible colours. Red has the longest wavelength (~620–750 nm) and lowest frequency. This is why UV (beyond violet) causes sunburn while IR (beyond red) is merely heat.

questions.text: A concave mirror has focal length 15 cm. An object is placed 45 cm in front of it (u = −45 cm, f = −15 cm). Using the mirror formula, the image distance v is ____.

options.text: v = −22.5 cm (real image, 22.5 cm in front)
v = −30 cm (real image, 30 cm in front of mirror)
v = −45 cm (real image at same position as object)
v = +22.5 cm (virtual image, 22.5 cm behind mirror)

questions.explanation: Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u → 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/(−15) − 1/(−45) = −3/45 + 1/45 = −2/45. So v = −45/2 = −22.5 cm. Negative v confirms a real image formed in front of the concave mirror. The image is between the centre of curvature (30 cm) and the focus (15 cm), hence magnified.

questions.text: Light passes from glass (refractive index 1.5) to air. sin C = 1/1.5, giving critical angle C ≈ 42°. A ray hits the glass–air interface at 45°. What happens?

options.text: C ≈ 42°; the ray undergoes total internal reflection at 45°
C ≈ 48°; the ray refracts partially into air at 45°
C ≈ 42°; the ray refracts and partially reflects at 45°
C ≈ 48°; the ray undergoes total internal reflection at 45°

questions.explanation: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667 → C ≈ 41.8° ≈ 42°. Since the incident angle (45°) > critical angle (42°), the condition for TIR is met — the ray reflects entirely back into the glass with no refraction into air. This is why optical fibre cores (denser glass) confine light by TIR at the glass–cladding interface.
